sections.heading: 2 Setting
sections.text: We start with introducing our notation. The marginal and conditional probabilities under the probability measure p p are p ⁡ ( X = x ) p(X=x) and p ⁡ ( X = x ∣ Y = y ) p(X=x\mid Y=y) , respectively; and we write p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) and p ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) p(x\mid y) when the random variables are clear from context. The indicator function is { ⋅ } \mathds{1}\!\left\{\cdot\right\} . For a positive integer n n , we define [ n ] = { 1 , … , n } [n]=\left\{1,\dots,n\right\} . We denote the i i -th entry of vector v v by v i v_{i} . If the vector is already indexed, such as v j v_{j} , we write v j , i v_{j,i} . We consider a general reinforcement learning problem ( Sutton and Barto, 1998 ) where an agent interacts with an environment in an episode consisting of multiple steps. The agent takes actions conditioned on the interaction history and the environment responds. When the episode ends, it is assigned a reward. The reward measures the quality of the interaction and the agent maximizes it. We formalize the problem as follows. The agent first observes context x ∈ 𝒮 x\in\mathcal{S} , where 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is the space of all token sequences. The context defines the task. The interaction between the agent and environment consists of steps indexed by t ∈ ℕ t\in\mathbb{N} , where ℕ \mathbb{N} is a set of positive integers. At step t t , the agent takes an action a t ∈ 𝒮 a_{t}\in\mathcal{S} and the environment responds with an observation y t ∈ 𝒮 y_{t}\in\mathcal{S} . The interaction history up to step n n is a trajectory τ n = ( a 1 , y 1 , … , a n , y n ) \tau_{n}=(a_{1},y_{1},\dots,a_{n},y_{n}) of n n actions and observations. We assume that the number of steps n n is fixed. The reward is a non-negative function of x x and τ n \tau_{n} , denoted by r ⁡ ( x , τ n ) ≥ 0 r(x,\tau_{n})\geq 0 , and measures the quality of the interaction. We do not make any additional assumptions on the reward. This is to maintain generality and because our algorithms ( Section 3 ) do not require it. The agent follows a policy conditioned on its history. Specifically, the probability that action a a is taken in context x x and history τ t − 1 \tau_{t-1} is π ⁡ ( a ∣ x , τ t − 1 ; θ ) \pi(a\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta) , and is parameterized by θ ∈ Θ \theta\in\Theta . We call θ \theta a policy and Θ \Theta the space of policy parameters. The probability of observing y t y_{t} conditioned on history τ t − 1 \tau_{t-1} and action a t a_{t} is denoted by p ⁡ ( y t ∣ x , τ t − 1 , a t ) p(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1},a_{t}) . We slightly abuse our notation and denote the probability of trajectory τ n \tau_{n} in context x x under policy θ \theta by π ⁡ ( τ n ∣ x ; θ ) = ∏ t = 1 n p ⁡ ( y t ∣ x , τ t − 1 , a t ) ​ π ​ ( a t ∣ x , τ t − 1 ; θ ) . \displaystyle\pi(\tau_{n}\mid x;\theta)=\prod_{t=1}^{n}p(y_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1},a_{t})\,\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta)\,. The factorization follows from the chain rule of probability. The expected value of policy θ \theta , where q q is a distribution over contexts x x , is defined as V ( θ ) = 𝔼 x ∼ q , τ n ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ x ; θ ) [ r ( x , τ n ) ] . \displaystyle V(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim q,\,\tau_{n}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x;\theta)}\left[r(x,\tau_{n})\right]\,. (1) Our goal is to learn a policy θ ∗ = arg ​ max θ ∈ Θ ⁡ V ​ ( θ ) \theta_{*}=\argmax_{\theta\in\Theta}V(\theta) with the highest expected value. Our formulation is more general than those in the closest related works, which focused only on specific policies and did not consider observations ( Kveton et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Our framework can model multiple use cases. For instance, suppose that we want to maximize the pedagogical value of a conversation over n n steps ( Scarlatos et al., 2025 ) . Then τ n \tau_{n} is an n n -step conversation and r ⁡ ( x , τ n ) r(x,\tau_{n}) is its pedagogical value. We experiment with such problems in Section 5 . In math reasoning problems ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , τ n \tau_{n} would be agent’s reasoning and r ⁡ ( x , τ n ) r(x,\tau_{n}) would indicate whether its response is correct.

sections.heading: 3.2 Partial Policy Gradient
sections.text: While the gradient in ( 2 ) is valid, the reward is attributed equally to each step, since all ∇ log ⁡ π ​ ( a t ∣ x , τ t − 1 ; θ ) \nabla\log\pi(a_{t}\mid x,\tau_{t-1};\theta) are multiplied by the same reward r ⁡ ( x , τ n ) r(x,\tau_{n}) . If the attribution could be improved, we could reduce the variance in estimator ( 3 ) and improve statistical efficiency. We propose a general attribution framework that allows for such tradeoffs. The framework has two components. Factored reward. We assume that the reward factors as r ⁡ ( x , τ n ) = ∑ t = 1 n r t , r 1 , … , r n ≥ 0 , \displaystyle r(x,\tau_{n})=\sum_{t=1}^{n}r_{t}\,,\quad r_{1},\dots,r_{n}\geq 0\,, (4) where r t = r ⁡ ( x , τ t ) r_{t}=r(x,\tau_{t}) denotes the reward at step t t , and is a function of x x and τ t \tau_{t} . The reward r t r_{t} with such properties can be either observed, for instance if the environment is an MDP with per-step rewards, or designed. We present a general design that guarantees ( 4 ) next.

sections.heading: 5.1 Data Settings
sections.text: Problem Formulation. Our learning problem is maintaining consistent and faithful human personas over time in role-playing dialogues like therapy, education, and chatting. We instantiate the framework in Section 2 as follows. The context x x is a persona definition given at the start of the interaction in a system prompt. A trajectory τ n \tau_{n} is a dialogue history between an LLM-simulated agent and the environment . The agent’s responses are actions a t a_{t} and the environment’s replies are observations y t y_{t} . Dataset. We experiment with Consistent-LLMs benchmark ( Abdulhai et al., 2025 ) , which provides human-persona dialogues across 3 distinct domains: (i) Education: Tutoring sessions where a student agent maintains specific learning preferences and the tutor acts as the environment; (ii) Therapy: Counseling sessions where a patient agent maintains consistent mental health backgrounds while the therapist serves as the environment; and (iii) Chatting: Casual dialogue where a simulated human is the agent maintaining biographical consistency (family, career, and so on) against a conversational environment. Each domain comprises of 6 500 6\,500 trajectories ( 5 200 5\,200 training and 1 300 1\,300 test) of varying lengths ( 2 2 to 60 60 steps, with 23 23 steps on average). The trajectories are generated using a Llama-3.1-8B model.

sections.heading: 5.2 Evaluation
sections.text: Abdulhai et al. (2025) proposed two metrics to evaluate role-playing consistency: (i) Prompt consistency measures if an agent’s response aligns with their assigned persona or background. (ii) Index consistency evaluates if an agent’s response contradicts to their own previous responses in the conversation history based on their past prompt consistency scores. Since index consistency is a secondary metric derived from prompt consistency, we use prompt consistency in our work; and call it persona consistency (PC) because it measures the consistency of a persona. Using this terminology, the reward at step t t , r t = r ⁡ ( x , τ t ) r_{t}=r(x,\tau_{t}) , is its PC. All policies are learned offline from the training trajectories of Abdulhai et al. (2025) . At test time, we measure the PC using an LLM judge with the same prompts as in Abdulhai et al. (2025) . Specifically, for each agent’s response a t a_{t} , we ask the LLM judge to evaluate if it contradicts the persona description provided as context x x and score it 1 1 (consistent) if the judge outputs “NO” (no contradiction) or 0 0 (inconsistent) if the judge outputs “YES” (contradiction detected). The judge is implemented using GPT-4o mini with temperature 0 0 , and we report the mean scores across all steps of the evaluated trajectories. See prompts in Appendix E . We employ two complementary evaluation protocols to assess persona consistency under different distribution conditions. The first follows the rollout methodology from Abdulhai et al. (2025) , while the second is designed to isolate consistency improvements from error propagation effects. Rollout evaluation. Following Abdulhai et al. (2025) , we generate complete conversation trajectories starting with only the initial persona description as context, alternating between responses of the agent and a fixed simulated environment implemented using Llama-3.1-70B model. This exposes the agent to distribution shifts, as inconsistencies compound over time, making it a challenging test of maintaining long-horizon consistency. Step-level evaluation. To disentangle consistency improvements from error compounding, we introduce a controlled evaluation setting where each step is assessed independently. Specifically, we take the test trajectories of Abdulhai et al. (2025) and for each step in them, we generate the response of the agent given the conversation history of that particular trajectory. This design isolates the model’s inherent consistency capability from the cascading effects of its own errors without model-induced distribution shift.

sections.heading: 5.3 Baselines and Compared Methods
sections.text: We have two baselines. 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base is an unmodified base model used zero-shot to show what can be attained without learning. PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) was used as a policy optimization algorithm in Abdulhai et al. (2025) , and hence is a state-of-the-art baseline in our domain. We experiment with two agent models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, which we abbreviate as Qwen and Llama , respectively. All our policies are learned offline by an offline policy gradient ( Section 3.4 ), where ρ \rho samples trajectories uniformly at random from the training set. The reward at step t t is the persona consistency at step t t ( Section 5.2 ). The rewards are standardized as in ( 9 ). We learn a full planning policy ( 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG in Section 4.1 ), greedy policy ( 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG in Section 4.2 ), and K K -step lookahead policies ( 𝙺 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG in Section 4.3 ) for K = { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } K=\{2,3,4,5\} . sections.heading: 5.4 Main Results
sections.text: We start by evaluating all policies in all domains: education , therapy , and chatting ; and report their average persona consistency in Tables 1 , 2 and 3 . While the best performing policy is domain-dependent, policy gradients universally outperform 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base and PPO, demonstrating the robustness of offline RL by policy gradients. In chatting and therapy domains, K K -step lookahead policies ( 𝟸 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG ) perform extremely well across both Qwen and Llama models. 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG is the best policy in the education domain, because a faithful simulation of a tutored student requires long-term planning. We observe consistent results across rollout and step-level evaluation methodologies, suggesting that our gains are robust despite the cascading errors commonly observed in long dialogues. Our results show similar trends for both Qwen and Llama models, suggesting that our approach generalizes across multiple LLM architectures.

sections.heading: 5.5 On Effectiveness of Simpler Policies
sections.text: Now we try to understand the best performing policies. For all policies, we compute the mean persona consistency at each conversation step, subtract the mean over all steps, and renormalize to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] jointly over all policies. Note that this is just a linear transformation of consistency scores that makes them comparable across the policies. We call this quantity a residual and report it in Figure 2 . The residual of 𝙱𝚊𝚜𝚎 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt Base monotonically decreases as conversation progresses, confirming that LLMs are susceptible to persona drift in long-horizon conversations ( Nie et al., 2021 ) . The residual of 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG oscillates a lot. These ripples reflect the policy’s repeated failed recovery attempts from persona drift, due to not planning for the future. In comparison, K K -step lookahead policies ( 𝙺 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG ) maintain stable residuals across trajectory steps. We observe that increasing K K from K = 1 K=1 ( 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG ) to K = 3 K=3 ( 𝙺 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt K\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG ) produces progressively smoother residuals, supporting our theory that assigning credit to longer horizons can prevent persona drift by maintaining consistency continuously over time. Finally, in therapy and chatting domains, we observe that 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG oscillates a lot and thus performs worse than 𝟹 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG . This experiment shows that the temporal scope of credit assignment directly influences policy stability, with longer horizons providing smoother and more robust behavior at the cost of increased data requirements. Results for Llama are in Appendix D . See qualitative analysis in Appendix G .

sections.heading: 5.6 On Statistical Efficiency of Simpler Policies
sections.text: We investigate the statistical efficiency of learning different policies next. Specifically, we vary the number of training trajectories, from 50 50 (low-data regime, 1 % 1\% of training data) to 5 000 5\,000 (high-data regime, all training data), and plot the persona consistency of all policies in Figure 3 . Our results reveal a fundamental trade-off between policy complexity and statistical efficiency. In the low-data regime, 𝙶𝚛𝚎𝚎𝚍𝚢𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt GreedyPG consistently excels in all domains, confirming our hypothesis that simpler policies are easier to learn when data are scarce. As data scales to moderate levels ( 500 500 trajectories, 10 % 10\% of training data), K K -step lookahead policies dominate across all domains. In particular, 𝟸 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 2\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG and 𝟹 − 𝚂𝚝𝚎𝚙 − 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt 3\mathchar 45\relax Step\mathchar 45\relax PG are the best policies in therapy and chatting domains. These policies strike balance between planning enough for the future and being able to learn it. In the education domain, we observe that full planning with 𝙿𝙶 \color[rgb]{0,1,0}\tt PG eventually achieves the highest persona consistency in the high-data regime. We validate this scaling behavior across three model architectures (Llama, Qwen, Gemma) on an additional dataset (Synthetic Persona Chat ( Jandaghi et al., 2024 ) ) in Appendix B , confirming that optimal lookahead horizon K K consistently increases with available training data, establishing a practical design principle for calibrating policy complexity to data budgets.
